---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
{\bf CZF} + {\bf AC} derives the law of excluded middle $\phi \vee \neg \phi $ for $\Delta_0$-formulas $\phi$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
See \cite{AczelRath}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
In \cite{AczelRath}, it is shown that this proof can be carried out in a weaker subsystem of {\bf CZF}. On the other hand, the weaker principles of {\it countable choice} and {\it dependent choice} can be added to {\bf CZF} without leading to undesirable results.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Real numbers both as Dedekind cuts or as Cauchy's sequences form a set in {\bf CZF}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
See \cite{AczelRath}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
The type-theoretic Axiom of Choice 
\begin{equation*}
    ({\bf AC})\ \Pi_{(x:A)}\ \Sigma_{(y:B)}\ R(x,y)\ \rightarrow \Sigma_{(f: A \rightarrow B)}\ \Pi_{(x:A)}\ R(x,f(x))
\end{equation*}
where $A$ and $B$ are  sets (i.e. types) and $R$ any relation on them, 
    is derivable in \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{dedcut}
    A Dedekind cut on the rationals is a pair $(L,U)$ of subsets $L,U \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$ that satisfy the usual conditions of being inhabited, disjoint, open, monotone, and located, all defined as in \cite{maiettisambinhand}.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
We denote with $\mathbb{R}_{D_{k}}$  the support of Dedekind cuts made
of propositional functions with values in the universe $U_k$ for any natural number $k$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{bijdedcau}
    In \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}, Dedekind reals $\mathbb{R}_{D_{0}}$ are in bijective correspondence with the Cauchy reals, defined as Cauchy sequences à la Bishop.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
See  Prop.17 in \cite{CN95} and section 4.3 of \cite{MSpointfree}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{dedres}
 In \mbox{{\bf MLTT}},  the set $\mathbb{R}_{D_{0}}$ of Dedekind reals is   in bijective correspondence with the set of Dedekind reals $\mathbb{R}_{D_{k}}$  for any natural number $k$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Given a Dedekind cut as in def.~\ref{dedcut} in $\mathbb{R}_{D_{k}}$  for any natural 
   number $k$, by using the axiom of choice we can define a Bishop real given by an operation
   $\lambda n. x_n $, usually written $(x_n)_{n}$, as in Prop. 17 in \cite{CN95} or section 4.3 in \cite{MSpointfree}, whose 
   cut $(L_0, D_0)$ in $\mathbb{R}_{D_{0}}$ is defined as

$$L_0\equiv \{ p : \mathbb{Q}\ \mid\ \Sigma_{n : \mathbb{N}}\ p\leq x_n-2/n \ \}\qquad\qquad  U_0\equiv \{ q: \mathbb{Q}\ \mid\ \Sigma_{n: \mathbb{N}}\ q\geq x_n +2/n \ \}$$
  
  \noindent and is propositionally equivalent to the starting cut $(L,U)$ in $\mathbb{R}_{D_{k}}$ thanks
   to the correspondence between Dedekind cuts, formal points of point-free topology of real numbers and Bishop reals in 
   section 4.3 of \cite{MSpointfree}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The previous proposition resembles a special case of  Russell's Reducibility Axiom which constructively requires  a  choice principle to be derived.  If the law of excluded middle were valid the full Reducibility axiom would follow as shown in section 5.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{unipri}
    {\bf AC!} can be derived in {\bf HoTT}.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
See \cite{rijke2015sets}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Unique existence can be formulated in an equivalent way in {\bf HoTT}\ by employing the notion of contractible type. A type $A$ is said to be contractible if the following type is inhabited: 

    \begin{equation*}
        \Sigma_{(x:A)}\ \Pi_{(y:A)}\ x =_A y.
    \end{equation*}
Therefore, we can rewrite unique choice by requiring the contractibility of $\Sigma_{(y:B)}\  R(x,y)$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The proof of {\bf AC!} in \cite{rijke2015sets}  is a special case of a result that holds in the internal dependent type theory $\mathcal{T}_{reg}$ of any regular category \cite{Maietti05}. Following \cite{Maietti05}, observe that the propositional truncation of a $\Sigma$-type $\Sigma_{(x:A)}\ P(x)$ can be equivalently expressed in $\mathcal{T}_{reg}$  as a quotient, namely the quotient $\Sigma_{(x:A)}\ P(x)/\mathbf{1}$ over the unit type identifying all the proof-terms. 
    Then, the proof in \cite{rijke2015sets} corresponds to the argument in \cite{Maietti05} relying on the fact that unique existence can be written as $\Sigma_{(y:B)}\ R(x,y)$ together with the usual uniqueness condition. In this case, $\Sigma_{(y:B)}\ R(x,y)$ is a mono type, according to the terminology introduced in \cite{Maietti05}, and is equivalent to its quotient over the unit type, and hence we can use $\Sigma$-projections to prove {\bf AC!}.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
The {\em internal rule of unique choice}, called ${\bf iRC!}$,  is formulated for ${\bf HA^\omega}$ as follows: 
\begin{equation*}
    \mbox{if}\ \ {\bf HA^\omega} \vdash \forall x^\sigma \ \exists ! y^\tau \ \phi(x,y) \qquad  \mbox{then}\ \ {\bf HA^\omega} \vdash \exists f^{\sigma \rightarrow \tau}\ \forall x^\sigma \ \phi(x,fx)
\end{equation*}
where $\exists ! y^\tau \ \phi(x,y)\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \exists y^\tau \ \phi(x,y) \land \forall y_1^\tau \ \forall y_2^\tau \ (\ \phi(x,y_1) \ \land\  \phi(x,y_2)\ \supset\ y_1 =_\tau y_2)$. 
\vspace{0.6em}

The special case when ${\bf iRC!}$ acts only on natural numbers, namely both $\sigma$ and $\tau$ coincide with the type $\mathbf{N}$ of natural numbers, 
is called {\it internal number-theoretic rule of unique choice} and it is denoted with the symbol ${\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}}$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
We call the rule displayed above {\it internal} rule of unique choice to contrast it with the following {\it rule of  unique choice}: if $ {\bf HA^\omega} \ \vdash\  \forall x^\sigma \ \exists ! y^\tau\
     \phi(x,y)$, then there exists a function $f^{\sigma \ \rightarrow \ \tau}$ such that $ {\bf HA^\omega} \ \vdash\ \forall x^\sigma \ \phi(x, fx)$,  where the existence of the choice function is stated externally.
    Admittedly, in  $ {\bf HA^\omega}$ the two rules are equivalent by the results in \cite{troelstra1973}. In general, this equivalence holds for all the systems that satisfy the existence property, but it cannot be stated in general. For instance, it does not hold for classical systems.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{CA} The theory ${\bf HA^\omega} + {\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}} + {\bf LEM}$ derives the second-order comprehension principle ${\bf CA}$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let us consider a formula $\phi(x)$ with $x$ of type $\mathbf{N}$. Then, we can define the following relation 

    \begin{equation*}
        \chi_\phi (x,y)\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ (\phi(x)\ \land\ y^\mathbf{N} = 1)\ \lor\ (\neg \phi(x)\ \land\ y^\mathbf{N} = 0)
    \end{equation*}

    By the validity of {\bf LEM}, we can argue by cases: 

    \begin{itemize}
        \item[--] if $\phi(x)$ holds, then $\chi_\phi (x,1)$ holds.

        \item[--] if $\neg \phi(x)$ holds, then $\chi_\phi(x,0)$ holds. 
    \end{itemize}

    We recall that $0 \neq 1$ follows from the axioms of ${\bf HA^\omega}$. Thus we obtain $\forall x^\mathbf{N}\ \exists ! y^\mathbf{N}\ \chi_\phi (x,y)$, that is a functional relation. 

    Therefore, we can apply ${\bf iRC!}_{\mathbf{N}, \mathbf{N}}$  and we obtain that 

    \begin{equation*}
        \exists f^{\mathbf{N} \rightarrow \mathbf{N}}\ \forall x^\mathbf{N}\ \chi_\phi (x, fx)
    \end{equation*}

    which, unfolding the definition of $\chi_\phi$, amounts to 

    \begin{equation*}
        \exists  f^{\mathbf{N} \rightarrow \mathbf{N}}\ \forall x^\mathbf{N}\ ((\phi(x)\ \land\ fx=1)\ \lor\ (\neg \phi(x)\ \land\ fx = 0))
    \end{equation*}

    From which {\bf CA} follows.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{inchao}
    The theory ${\bf PA}^2$ can be interpreted within ${\bf HA^\omega} + {\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}} + {\bf LEM}$, which is then impredicative and incompatible with Weyl's predicativity.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
A compatible translation from ${\bf HA}^\omega + {\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}}$ to \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}\ can be defined as follows: 

\begin{itemize}
    \item[-] $(\mathbf{N})^\ast\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \mathbb{N}$, while $(\sigma \rightarrow \tau)^\ast\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \sigma^\ast \rightarrow \tau^\ast$ and $(\sigma \times \tau)^\ast\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \sigma^\ast \times \tau^\ast$. 

    \item[-] variables $x: \sigma$ are translated as variables $x: \sigma^\ast$ and application terms as application terms in \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}.

    \item[-] constants of ${\bf HA}^\omega$ are translated as the corresponding terms in \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}: e.g., $(\textbf{k})^\ast {\ :\equiv\ } \lambda x. \lambda y.x: \sigma^\ast \rightarrow (\tau^\ast \rightarrow \sigma^\ast)$.

    \item[-] the formulas of many-sorted intuitionistic logic are sent to the corresponding types according to the propositions-as-types principle: e.g., $(\exists x^\sigma\ \phi(x))^\ast\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \Sigma_{(x:\sigma^\ast)}\ \phi^\ast(x)$. 
    
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{hamltt}
    The translation $(-)^\ast$ is a compatible translation of ${\bf HA}^\omega + {\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}}$ in \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The proof is by induction over the structure of derivations. In particular, the interpretation of the number-theoretic internal rule of unique choice follows from the validity of the more general rule of choice in \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\mbox{{\bf MLTT}}\ + {\bf LEM} becomes impredicative.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
It follows from Prop.~\ref{hamltt} and Cor.~\ref{inchao}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
In general, in \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}\ with classical logic we can use the type of booleans {\bf 2} as a classifier, however we do not get a (strong) power object. For instance, the type $\mathbb{N} \rightarrow {\bf 2}$ behaves more like a {\it weak power object}, because \mbox{{\bf MLTT}}\ lacks of the relevant extensionality principles.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{comphot}
     The translation $(-)^\ast$ is a compatible translation of ${\bf HA}^\omega + {\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}}$ in {\bf HoTT}.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
{\bf HoTT}\ with the addition of the law of excluded middle for h-propositions becomes impredicative.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
It follows from  Prop.~\ref{comphot} and Cor.~\ref{inchao}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
When {\bf HoTT}\ is extended with {\bf LEM} for h-propositions, it is possible to show that the type of h-propositions within any universe $\mathcal{U}$, that is $\mathsf{Prop}_{\mathcal{U}}$, is equivalent (and hence equal by Univalence) to the type of Booleans {\bf 2} in $\mathcal{U}$. Therefore, {\bf 2} behaves like a {\it subobject classifier} and we can prove that the category of h-sets, as defined in \cite{hottbook}, is an elementary topos.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A compatible translation from ${\bf HA}^\omega + {\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}}$ to 
{\bf CZF}\ can be defined as follows: 

\begin{itemize}
    \item[-] $(\mathbf{N})^\ast\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \omega$, while $(\sigma \rightarrow \tau)^\ast\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \sigma^\ast \rightarrow \tau^\ast$, which is the set of functional relations from $\sigma^\ast$ to $\tau^\ast$, and $(\sigma \times \tau)^\ast\ {\ :\equiv\ }\ \sigma^\ast \times \tau^\ast$, which is the usual cartesian product of sets. 

    \item[-] terms of $\mathbf{HA}^\omega$ are interpreted by the corresponding definable terms of {\bf CZF}. 

    
\item [-] the formulas of many-sorted intutionistic logic are interpreted by the corresponding formulas of intuitionistic logic, with sorts interpreted as predicates: e.g., $(\forall x^\sigma\ \phi(x))^\ast {\ :\equiv\ } \forall x\ ( x \in \sigma^\ast\ \rightarrow\ \phi^\ast(x))$.

\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{compczf}
    The translation $(-)^\ast$ is a compatible translation of ${\bf HA}^\omega + {\bf iRC!_{\mathbf{N},\mathbf{N}}}$ in {\bf CZF}.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
{\bf CZF} with the addition of the law of excluded middle becomes impredicative.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
It follows from  Prop.~\ref{compczf} and Cor.~\ref{inchao}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
The axiom of exponentiation and the law of excluded middle for $\Delta_0$-formulas imply the powerset axiom.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
It is enough to show that $\mathcal{P}(1)$ is a set. This follows from an application of {\bf LEM}.
    The rest follows from the fact that the powerset axiom is equivalent to exponentiation plus the existence of the powerset of the singleton set.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
{\bf CZF} with classical logic and {\bf ZF} prove the same set of theorems.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
See \cite{aczel78}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
In \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ the {\it internal rule of unique choice}  holds if for any derivable small proposition
    \begin{equation*}
        R(x,y)\ prop_s\ [ x \in A, y\in B]
    \end{equation*}
    and for any derivable judgement of the form 
   \begin{equation*}
        p(x) \in \exists !_{ y\in B}\  R(x,y)\ [x \in A]
    \end{equation*}
 there exists a proof-term $q$ such that the following judgement is derivable
\begin{equation*}
    q \in\exists_{f\in A\rightarrow B}\ \forall_{x\in A} \ R(\, x,\mathsf{Ap}(f,x)\, )\ \
\end{equation*}

We call  {\it number-theoretic internal rule of unique choice} the instance of the internal rule of unique choice when $A$ and $B$ coincide with the set $\mathsf{N}$ of natural numbers.

Instead, we reserve the name {\it rule of unique choice} for the version of the above rule requiring
the external existence of the choice function term $f$, i.e. if $\exists !_{ y\in B}\  R(x,y)\ [x \in A]$ holds then we can derive a term $f\in A\rightarrow B$ such that
$R(\, x,\mathsf{Ap}(f,x)\, )\ [x\in A]
$ holds.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{norun}
The rule of unique choice
is not valid in \mbox{{\bf mTT}}.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
See proof of Th.1 of \cite{Ma17}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{rulax}
    If \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ satisfies the internal rule of unique choice, then it satisfies the axiom of unique choice.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The proof of Prop.3  in \cite{Ma17} can be easily adapted to the case of the internal rule of unique choice.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{coruc}
    \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ does not validate the internal rule of unique choice.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{equi} Both levels of {\bf MF}\ are equiconsistent with \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ extended  the addition of the law of excluded middle $\phi \vee \neg \phi$ for all propositions $\phi$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
For a proof, we refer to \cite{MSdoubleneg}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{boun} The proof-theoretic strength of both levels of {\bf MF}\ are bounded by Feferman's theory $\widehat{ID_1}$ of non-iterative fixpoints.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{bouncla} The proof-theoretic strength of the classical extension of {\bf MF}\ is  bounded by Feferman's theory $\widehat{ID_1}$ of non-iterative fixpoints.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
It follows from Prop.\ref{equi} and  Prop.\ref{boun}.



From this, knowing that  {\bf HA$^\omega$} can be  embedded in \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ and \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ 
in a compatible way, we can deduce the non-derivability of  unique choice on natural numbers in their
classical version:
\begin{corollary}\label{norucla}
The classical versions of \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ and \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ do not validate the number-theoretic
internal rule of choice and hence the number-theoretic axiom of unique choice:
\begin{equation*}\label{uniquenat}
 ({\bf AC!_{\mathsf{N},\mathsf{N}}})\    \forall_{x\in \mathsf{N}}\ \exists !_{y\in \mathsf{N}}\ R(x,y)\ \rightarrow\ \exists_{f\in \mathsf{N} \rightarrow \mathsf{N}}\ \forall_{x\in \mathsf{N}}\ R(x,f(x))
\end{equation*}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
First, observe that $\bf AC!_{\mathsf{N},\mathsf{N}}$ implies the number-theoretic internal rule of unique choice. The claim then follows from Proposition~\ref{bouncla} and Cor.~\ref{inchao}.
\end{proof}
Since the validity of the axiom of unique choice  in a theory can be transferred to its extensions, contrary to the rule of unique choice, 
from Cor.~\ref{norucla} we can immediately deduce the non-validity of ${\bf AC!_{\mathsf{N},\mathsf{N}}}$
in \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ and \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ themselves:
\begin{corollary}
Both \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ and of \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ do not validate the number-theoretic axiom of unique choice.
\end{corollary}


\noindent It is worth noting that in the extensional level \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ of {\bf MF}\ we can also interpret the intuitionistic version of {\bf ACA}  in a way that preserves the meaning of all logical operators:

\begin{proposition}\label{acint}
The  intuitionistic version of {\bf ACA} is interpretable in the extensional level \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\  of {\bf MF}. Hence,  (the classical) {\bf ACA} can be interpreted in the classical version of \mbox{{\bf emTT}}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
It is sufficient to define a translation from {\bf ACA} to \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ as follows. Numerical variables of {\bf ACA} are translated as variables of type $\mathsf{N}$ in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}. Set variables of {\bf ACA} are translated as terms of type $ \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$. The symbols for zero and the successor in {\bf ACA} are interpreted by the corresponding constructors for $\mathsf{N}$ in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}. Atomic formulas of the form $s = t$ are translated as propositional equalities over $\mathsf{N}$ and those of the form $t \in X$ as small propositions $t\ \varepsilon\ X$\footnote{This notation can be defined in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}. Given $X \in \mathcal{P}(A)$ and $t \in A$, we define $t\ \varepsilon\ X$ as $\mathsf{Eq}(\mathcal{P}(1), X(t), [ \top])$. Moreover, it holds that $t\ \varepsilon\ \{x \in A \mid \phi(x) \} \leftrightarrow \phi(t) $ is true. }. In general, first-order formulas of {\bf ACA} are translated as small propositions with quantifiers ranging over $\mathsf{N}$, while second-order formulas are translated as propositions with quantifiers ranging over the collection $\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$. 

Peano axioms can be derived in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ thanks to the rules for $\mathsf{N}$ and the presence of $\mathcal{P}(1)$. In particular, the induction scheme of {\bf ACA} follows from the elimination rule for $\mathsf{N}$, which acts towards all collections, including propositions. 

Finally, the arithmetical comprehension axiom is validated as follows: given a small proposition $\phi(x)\ [x \in \mathsf{N}]$, we can introduce $[\phi(x)]\in \mathcal{P}(1)\ [x \in \mathsf{N}]$ and then form $\{ x \in \mathsf{N}\ \mid\ \phi(x)\} \in \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$. Then, it follows that there is an $X \in \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$ such that for all $x \in \mathsf{N}$, $x\ \varepsilon\ X\ \leftrightarrow\ \phi(x)$ holds.
\end{proof}
Hence, from  prop.~\ref{acint} it follows that the classical version of {\bf MF}\ can formalize Weyl's classical predicative reformulation of analysis in {\it Das Kontinuum} following Feferman's analysis in \cite{feferman1998light, feferman2000significance}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{norucla}
The classical versions of \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ and \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ do not validate the number-theoretic
internal rule of choice and hence the number-theoretic axiom of unique choice:
\begin{equation*}\label{uniquenat}
 ({\bf AC!_{\mathsf{N},\mathsf{N}}})\    \forall_{x\in \mathsf{N}}\ \exists !_{y\in \mathsf{N}}\ R(x,y)\ \rightarrow\ \exists_{f\in \mathsf{N} \rightarrow \mathsf{N}}\ \forall_{x\in \mathsf{N}}\ R(x,f(x))
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
First, observe that $\bf AC!_{\mathsf{N},\mathsf{N}}$ implies the number-theoretic internal rule of unique choice. The claim then follows from Proposition~\ref{bouncla} and Cor.~\ref{inchao}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
Both \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ and of \mbox{{\bf mTT}}\ do not validate the number-theoretic axiom of unique choice.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{acint}
The  intuitionistic version of {\bf ACA} is interpretable in the extensional level \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\  of {\bf MF}. Hence,  (the classical) {\bf ACA} can be interpreted in the classical version of \mbox{{\bf emTT}}.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
It is sufficient to define a translation from {\bf ACA} to \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ as follows. Numerical variables of {\bf ACA} are translated as variables of type $\mathsf{N}$ in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}. Set variables of {\bf ACA} are translated as terms of type $ \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$. The symbols for zero and the successor in {\bf ACA} are interpreted by the corresponding constructors for $\mathsf{N}$ in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}. Atomic formulas of the form $s = t$ are translated as propositional equalities over $\mathsf{N}$ and those of the form $t \in X$ as small propositions $t\ \varepsilon\ X$\footnote{This notation can be defined in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}. Given $X \in \mathcal{P}(A)$ and $t \in A$, we define $t\ \varepsilon\ X$ as $\mathsf{Eq}(\mathcal{P}(1), X(t), [ \top])$. Moreover, it holds that $t\ \varepsilon\ \{x \in A \mid \phi(x) \} \leftrightarrow \phi(t) $ is true. }. In general, first-order formulas of {\bf ACA} are translated as small propositions with quantifiers ranging over $\mathsf{N}$, while second-order formulas are translated as propositions with quantifiers ranging over the collection $\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$. 

Peano axioms can be derived in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ thanks to the rules for $\mathsf{N}$ and the presence of $\mathcal{P}(1)$. In particular, the induction scheme of {\bf ACA} follows from the elimination rule for $\mathsf{N}$, which acts towards all collections, including propositions. 

Finally, the arithmetical comprehension axiom is validated as follows: given a small proposition $\phi(x)\ [x \in \mathsf{N}]$, we can introduce $[\phi(x)]\in \mathcal{P}(1)\ [x \in \mathsf{N}]$ and then form $\{ x \in \mathsf{N}\ \mid\ \phi(x)\} \in \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$. Then, it follows that there is an $X \in \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{N})$ such that for all $x \in \mathsf{N}$, $x\ \varepsilon\ X\ \leftrightarrow\ \phi(x)$ holds.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
In  the extensional level \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\  of {\bf MF}\ real numbers à la Dedekind or Cauchy do not form a set as well as in their classical version.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
A direct proof of this was given in \cite{ober2020}
but it follows also from the predicativity of the classical version of {\bf MF}\ (see also \cite{MSdoubleneg}). If real numbers form a set in {\bf MF}\ then this is so in the classical version of {\bf MF}\
and every interval of real numbers form a set too. Since classically,  the power-collection of natural numbers can be put in bijection with an interval of real numbers, then it would follow that impredicative definitions can be employed in the classical version of {\bf MF}\ contrary to its predicativity established 
 thanks in prop.\ref{bouncla}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
In  the extensional level \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\  of {\bf MF}\ the point-free topology of Dedekind real numbers and Cantor space are definable.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The formalization of the point-free topology of the Cantor space can be carried on in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ as in section 2.1 of \cite{Valentini-bar}.
Then, observe that the point-free topology of real numbers can be defined as in Def.3 of \cite{CN95}
in terms of another cover generated by a finite set of axioms that can be represented in \mbox{{\bf emTT}}\ with a completely analogous proof to that just mentioned for the point-free topology of  Cantor space.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
